fields.quote: Cedar Relay retries only eligible failures
Component study · Retry behavior
A retryability check stops retries after permanent failures, while the loop requests exponentially increasing delays before further attempts. Neither change guarantees exactly-once delivery.
Fictional change · Source and deterministic probe results
Based on the supplied source and modeled probes. No timing or production measurements; no separate verification findings were supplied.
The setting
One send, then a bounded retry budget

Cedar Relay wraps an asynchronous send operation with a retry loop. Previously, every rejection could trigger another attempt after a requested 10-millisecond delay. A successful send returned immediately; the final failed attempt threw its error. The retries argument counts extra attempts. With a budget of two, you can make at most three sends. A zero budget still allows the initial send.
The gap
Permanent failures still got another attempt

Send errors carry a boolean retryable property, but the old loop ignored it. In the supplied permanent-failure probe, the first send rejects with retryable: false. The old implementation requests a 10-millisecond sleep and sends again after that promise resolves; the new implementation rejects with that error after one call, without requesting sleep. The modeled sleep resolves immediately. This removes the extra attempt for a failure marked as permanent. The supplied contract does not identify who sets that classification. It does not establish whether a rejected send already changed the remote system.
The changed mechanism
Keep the bound, filter the error, double the delay

The updated loop preserves the attempt budget and awaits each send. Starting at zero makes the inclusive bound allow one initial attempt plus the configured retries. Returning the awaited result stops the loop on success. The catch block now decides whether another attempt is eligible before requesting a delay. A permanent error or exhausted budget throws immediately. Otherwise, the requested delays grow as 10, 20, 40 milliseconds, and so on. The exhaustion probe records three sends and delays of 10 and 20 milliseconds, versus 10 and 10 before. These are requested delays: the probe resolves sleep immediately. A rejected sleep propagates and prevents another send.
The short version
Better retry decisions, not exactly-once delivery

The change filters failures and increases requested retry delays within the existing budget. The author's exactly-once claim exceeds that mechanism: a remote effect can commit before a send rejects, and the duplicate probe records two effects in both implementations. There is no deduplication or idempotency contract. Separate calls share no retry counter, and no lock or cross-call delivery exclusion is supplied. The concurrent probe records an effect from each modeled call; it does not establish the internal state of an unshown send implementation.

fields.quote: Cedar Relay retries only eligible failures
Fictional change · Delivery retries

A retryability check stops retries after permanent failures, while exponential backoff increases requested delays before later attempts. These requests do not establish elapsed time. Neither change guarantees exactly-once delivery.
Source-based walkthrough · Deterministic local probes
Based on the supplied source and modeled probes. No production timing measurements or verification findings were supplied.
The setting
One send, then a bounded retry budget

Cedar Relay wraps an asynchronous send operation in a retry loop. You supply a nonnegative integer, retries, which counts extra attempts: a budget of two permits at most three sends. A successful send returns immediately. Previously, every send rejection with budget remaining triggered a requested 10-millisecond sleep. Another attempt followed only if that sleep fulfilled; a sleep rejection propagated instead.
The gap
Permanent failures could still get another attempt

The old loop ignored the rejection object's boolean retryable property. In the supplied permanent-failure scenario, it sends twice and reaches a modeled success after the first rejection. The changed loop instead rejects with the permanent error after one send, without sleeping. The send rejection's failure classification now controls retry eligibility, alongside the remaining budget.
The mechanism
Check eligibility before increasing the delay

The loop retains its original attempt boundary and success path: Starting at zero preserves the initial send even when retries is zero. The catch block now decides whether to continue: The guard rethrows a non-retryable error or the final attempt's error before sleeping. Otherwise, requested delays double: 10, 20, 40 milliseconds, and so on. With two retries exhausted, the probes record three sends and delays of 10 and 20, replacing 10 and 10. These are requested values; the probe resolves sleeps immediately and measures no elapsed time. A rejected sleep propagates and prevents another send.
The short version
Selective retries, not exactly-once delivery

The change filters retries and increases their requested spacing. The author's exactly-once claim does not follow: a send can commit remotely and then reject. The duplicate probe models that sequence and records two effects in both versions. No deduplication or idempotency contract prevents repetition. Separate calls also retain independent counters. The shown loop adds no lock, and no cross-call delivery exclusion is supplied by the contracts. The concurrent probe records two modeled effects; the underlying send implementation and its shared state are not shown. The improvement is a more selective retry policy, not a guarantee of one remote effect.
